_note: Same comparison through float64 L-BFGS. It agrees on the well-identified coefficients and the ATE, but drifts on rare one-hot levels along near-zero-curvature directions, hence the looser tolerances. max_abs_diff_named_coefs is the precision claim (Age, NIHSSa, treatment contrast, ~1e-3). max_abs_diff_flow_vs_statsmodels also spans the mRS_pre level contrasts, and level 5 has 7 of 1275 rows -- where two optimizers stop on it differs by ~0.1 between machines (0.028 here, 0.113 on the CI runner), so its bound is a sanity check. The flow's L-BFGS lands on a flat ridge (mRS_pre level 5 has 7 of 1275 rows), so its coefficients move by ~0.02 across machines while statsmodels and R do not; the {max} entries with a "why" carry that spread.

coef_Age_flow.why: 1.5x the ~0.02 cross-machine spread the _note records — 0.05 would let a near-zero Age coefficient pass

max_abs_diff_flow_vs_statsmodels.why: the maximum is over the mRS_pre level contrasts, and level 5 has 7 of 1275 rows: two optimizers place it ~0.1 apart across machines (0.028 here, 0.113 on the CI runner). max_abs_diff_named_coefs is the precision claim

ate_abs_diff_flow_vs_statsmodels.why: 0.0013 here, 0.0006 and 0.0032 on two CI runners — the same cross-machine L-BFGS spread; ate_flow's own atol 0.01 is the tighter claim

max_abs_diff_named_coefs.why: the same flat ridge as max_abs_diff_flow_vs_statsmodels reaches the named coefficients too: measured 0.0027 here (unchanged at 2 and 8 OMP threads) against 0.0018 and 0.0165 on two CI runners of the same image. L-BFGS in float64 is deterministic per machine, so the spread is the BLAS kernel, not the seed. The precision claim the file makes is coef_*_flow within atol 0.05 of R and statsmodels, and the ATE below

fit_seconds.why: 3x the 2-core CI runner measurement (7 s, 2026-09-01, tuned protocol): shared-runner wall clock is noisy, so this is a gross-regression tripwire, not a benchmark
